q: Are emissions from sending effluent to a common effluent treatment plant (CETP) my Scope 3?
title: Is effluent sent to a CETP my Scope 3?
short: Yes, in most cases. Effluent you send to a common effluent treatment plant (CETP) that you do not own or control is Scope 3 Category 5, waste generated in operations, under the GHG Protocol. Your share is the CETP's methane and energy use attributable to your effluent. Treatment inside your own fence stays in Scope 1 and 2.
audience: Textile, chemical, pharma and leather units in Indian clusters

sections.h: Where the line between scopes falls
ul: Your own primary treatment or ETP: methane from it is Scope 1, its electricity Scope 2.
A CETP run by a cluster society or SPV that you do not control: its emissions from treating your effluent are your Category 5.
Effluent to a municipal sewer and sewage treatment plant: also Category 5, since a third party treats it.
If you hold equity in the CETP SPV and report on the equity share approach, your share of the CETP's Scope 1 and 2 enters your own Scope 1 and 2; do not count the same emissions again in Category 5.
Sludge the CETP sends to a secured landfill or co-processing is part of the same treatment chain; include it in your Category 5 if the CETP reports it.

sections.h: Splitting the CETP's own figures among members
p: Many CETPs bill members by volume and pollution load, so they already measure inflow and inlet COD for each member. Ask the CETP for its annual electricity, any fuel, any biogas captured and its methane estimate, plus total inflow and total inlet COD.

Allocate methane by your share of COD, because methane comes from organic load. Allocate electricity and fuel by your share of volume, because pumping and aeration track flow. Write down both keys and keep them the same each year.

Estimate the methane from the COD you discharge with the IPCC 2006 Volume 5, Chapter 6 method: kg COD x 0.25 kg CH4 per kg COD x a methane correction factor from Table 6.8 that matches the CETP's process. Show a low and a high case, since the factor ranges from 0 for well managed aerobic treatment upwards. The wastewater methane page linked below works the method through step by step; the textile dyeing page adds ETP sludge and a full worked line.
For nitrous oxide, the 2006 Guidelines gave no method for industrial wastewater; the 2019 Refinement added one. Say which edition you used.

sections.h: Records an auditor will ask for
ul: CETP membership agreement and monthly charge invoices showing volume.
Your outlet flow meter log and COD test reports.
The CETP's annual totals and process description, or a note that it declined to share them.
The GWP edition used (IPCC AR5 or AR6) for converting methane to CO2e.

example.title: Worked example: allocating a CETP's reported totals (assumed figures)
lines: CETP year: 15,00,000 kL inflow, 30,00,000 kg inlet COD, 45,00,000 kWh electricity, 50,000 kg CH4 estimated by the CETP
Your unit: 60,000 kL and 90,000 kg COD; volume share 60,000 / 15,00,000 = 4%; COD share 90,000 / 30,00,000 = 3%
Methane: 50,000 x 3% = 1,500 kg CH4; at GWP 27 (IPCC AR6, non-fossil methane) = 40,500 kg CO2e
Your Category 5 line: 1,27,800 + 40,500 = 1,68,300 kg CO2e, about 168 t CO2e
example.note: All CETP and unit figures are assumed for illustration. Use the CETP's own annual totals and your billed volume and COD.

senseible: Senseible keeps CETP charge invoices in its separate Scope 3 evidence trail with the source file and SHA-256 fingerprint, and reads the CETP's electricity and fuel bills if it shares them. Methane needs COD and the treatment type, which come from your lab reports and the CETP; where only the charge is known, a spend-based estimate labelled as such can be provided.
